content: The document outlines the treatment guidelines and considerations for children and adolescents diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. 1. Decision-Making and PICO Questions: The guidelines address two primary questions for children and adolescents with chronic HCV: When is the optimal time to initiate treatment? Which direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimen should be used for treatment? 2. Population and Intervention: The population includes children aged 3–18 years with chronic HCV infection. For adolescents aged ≥12 years, treatment initiation with DAAs is compared to interferon (IFN)-based regimens. For children aged <12 years, the use of DAAs is not yet approved, and IFN-based therapies remain the only licensed option. 3. Outcomes of Interest: The outcomes include sustained virological response (SVR12), adverse events, treatment discontinuation, drug resistance, clinical outcomes, quality of life, pharmacokinetics (PK), transmission, costs, and cost-effectiveness. 4. Global Burden of Pediatric HCV: Approximately 5 million children aged 1–19 years are living with chronic HCV worldwide, with the majority of infections occurring in 19 countries. Transmission routes include blood transfusions, unsafe injections, and injecting drug use in adolescents. Despite global advancements in HCV treatment, children and adolescents remain underrepresented in treatment efforts. 5. Natural History of Pediatric HCV: Spontaneous viral clearance occurs in 7–20% of children, but most develop chronic infection. Liver fibrosis progression to cirrhosis is rare in children (2–3%), and end-stage liver disease during childhood is uncommon. However, hepatic fibrosis may progress during childhood, with some children showing increased severity of fibrosis over time. Groups at higher risk for rapid disease progression include children with thalassemia major, HIV co-infection, or a history of childhood cancer. 6. Current Treatment Options: DAAs for adults have been available since 2013, but their evaluation and approval for pediatric use have been delayed. In 2017, the FDA and EMA approved sofosbuvir/ledipasvir and sofosbuvir/ribavirin for adolescents aged ≥12 years or weighing ≥35 kg with specific HCV genotypes. For children aged <12 years, IFN-based therapies (pegylated IFN-α and ribavirin) remain the only approved treatment options, with treatment durations of 24–48 weeks depending on genotype. 7. Efficacy of DAAs in Adolescents: Clinical trials in adolescents aged 12–17 years have shown high SVR12 rates (98%) with sofosbuvir/ledipasvir and good tolerability. Common adverse events include headache, diarrhea, and fatigue, but no serious adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were reported. 8. Recommendations for Adolescents (≥12 years): For treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced adolescents with or without cirrhosis, the use of sofosbuvir/ledipasvir for 12 weeks is recommended for HCV genotypes 1, 4, 5, and 6. For genotypes 2 and 3, sofosbuvir with weight-based ribavirin for 12–24 weeks is recommended. 9. Recommendations for Children (<12 years): Treatment should be deferred until the child reaches 12 years of age, pending the approval of DAAs for younger age groups. IFN-based regimens should no longer be used due to their toxicity and lower efficacy. 10. Special Considerations: In exceptional cases, such as severe liver disease or high-risk groups (e.g., HIV co-infection, thalassemia major, childhood cancer survivors), IFN + ribavirin may be considered for children with genotypes 2 or 3. 11. Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: A systematic review compared the efficacy of DAAs versus pegylated IFN and ribavirin in children and adolescents. DAAs demonstrated significantly higher efficacy (98% SVR) compared to IFN-based regimens (90% for genotypes 2 and 3, 48% for genotypes 1 and 4). Adverse events and treatment discontinuation rates were lower with DAAs. 12. Ongoing Trials: Trials are ongoing to evaluate the use of DAAs in children aged 3–12 years, with preliminary results showing promising efficacy and safety profiles. 13. Conclusion: The introduction of DAAs for adolescents represents a significant advancement in the treatment of pediatric HCV. Efforts should focus on expanding access to DAAs for younger children and addressing the global burden of pediatric HCV to ensure equitable treatment opportunities.
